title: Om, from throat to lips
hookLine: why Nani starts every prayer with om, and a sound that walks across the mouth
carry: om: the one sound for brahman
tomorrow: how can one puff of breath turn a hand into something harsh?

lines: ONE SOUND WALKS THE WHOLE MAP.
cards: Open wide and say ahh, the way a doctor asks. That sound comes from the very back, the throat. Now close your lips and hum.

The front. Sanskrit lays out its letters exactly that way, throat first, lips last: a map of the mouth. And there's one sound Hindus say before almost every prayer that walks the whole map in a single breath: om.

teach.b: In the Katha Upanishad, a boy named Nachiketa waits three nights at the house of Death, unfed. When Yama, the lord of death, comes home, he offers the boy three wishes to make up for it.

For the last one, Nachiketa asks what nothing else can buy: what happens after death, and what lasts. Yama tries to talk him out of it. Take wealth, he says, long life, sons and grandsons, every pleasure.
The boy turns them all down.

teach.h: THE WORD ALL THE VEDAS POINT TO: OM.
teach.b: So Yama teaches him, and partway through he names the word that all the Vedas point toward: om. That syllable, Yama says, is Brahman, the reality behind everything.

teach.h: A, U, M, AND THE SILENCE AFTER.
teach.b: Another Upanishad, the Mandukya, hears om as three sounds, a, u and m, and the silence after. Feel it in your mouth. The a opens at the throat.
The u rounds the lips. The m closes them.
Throat to lips, the same road the alphabet takes, so many teachers read om as holding all of speech in one syllable.
The Mandukya matches a, u and m to waking, dreaming and deep sleep, and the silence after to the Self beyond all three.

That's why a puja, a prayer, a recitation of the Gita so often opens with om, and why a family chant can close om shanti shanti shanti. Before any words, the one sound that, the Upanishads say, points to everything.

how: Om is chanted at the start (and often the end) of Hindu prayers, pujas and recitations; the Mandukya Upanishad treats it as a, u, m and a silent fourth. Sanskrit's consonants are traditionally recited row by row, from the throat to the lips.

games.q: at a puja, everyone says om before the prayer. a friend asks why not just start the prayer. what fits the Upanishads?

games.why: Yama tells Nachiketa: the word all the Vedas point to is om, and that syllable is Brahman.

practice: Sit tall and breathe in. On the out-breath, chant om slowly, the way Hindus do before prayer: let the a open at the back of the throat, the u round the lips, the m close them into a hum you can feel in your face.
Then rest in the quiet after, the part the Mandukya calls the fourth. Do it a few times. If you'd rather not chant, just hum, and feel the sound travel forward.
